As a recipient of pages, I abhorred PagerDuty more than Slack, Teams, email or even phone calls. If your org is not mature enough to put in the time to have a single pane of glass, you shouldn't be buying any of these tools.
I think this is a better model than what I've seen setup in PD. Typically there was a fall-back escalation, and then it would go straight up the management chain, which seemed idiotic.

None of them have SCIM integration to make managing your teams automatic. All of them have clunky calendar overrides. For PagerDuty you need to call up their support team and get them to manually tweak something not in the UI settings to get OIDC for Azure AD sign-ins to work.
PagerDuty feels like abandonware. It hasn't changed in the last 4-5 years.

I run a service that integrates with pager duty... they have two versions of their event API, and keys for the v1 API don't work with v2 and vice versa... there's no way to distinguish what version a given key is for. I've already contacted support about it and their response has been, more or less, 'oh, uhhh... huh.'

PagerDuty is super expensive. A lot of the bells and whistles they have aren't useful. Engineers never need to actually use the PagerDuty website and only use the app for ack'ing the page. $100 a month per user on their enterprise plan is insane for what they offer.
I set my PagerDuty to the meow sound and I often refer to our processes as meow driven development as in I don't like my phone to meow desperately.
I can vouch that Support & Customer Success has always been a first class participant in the company. (Disclaimer: I worked at PagerDuty for 7+ happy years)

A user found PagerDuty underwhelming when their team moved to it. Calendar, holiday, workday and cross-regional scheduling were poorly implemented. Taking a week of vacation meant heavy manual schedule adjustment, "overrides on top of overrides", and negotiating rotation trades with teammates.

You only get value from PagerDuty in proportion to how much systems integration you do. If even one system still sends emails or Slack messages, or only updates a dashboard, PagerDuty becomes "yet-another-tool to monitor, rather than the single pane of glass."

A decade-long user didn't care for the UI ("Their UI is garbage"). They said PagerDuty succeeds because of "basically bulletproof reliability": "Pagerduty isn't perfect, but it was one of the most reliable services we ever used."

The PagerDuty app goes "directly from zero to klaxon", and the klaxons come from a "bizarrely limited menu" of horrible sounds. The user wants graduated escalation to the same person (vibrate, normal, critical, call). They also want a way to silence repeated notifications while already fixing an issue.

PagerDuty's pricing is called exorbitant. The user says the sales and account team forces year-long contracts for seats you don't need. Their team is "currently being threatened with an $8k bill because they claim we didn't 'cancel renewal' in time."

A user checked their bill and found they were paying $49 per user per month for features they don't need. Downgrading to the $29 tier requires contacting sales. "I'm furious. I won't downgrade. I'll cancel completely and move to your app."
Another commenter wrote: "Ever since their IPO they've been charging minibar rates for metric data storage."

With PagerDuty, you're mostly paying for reliability: "The peace of mind knowing that someone will get notified when there is an outage." The commenter says alert deliverability was the main problem it solved, with SMS and phone delivery. They believe that not being built on AWS meant alerts still arrived during AWS outages.

Frustrated by expensive per-seat pricing and unfriendly contract terms, one team looked for PagerDuty alternatives and adopted the open-source Uptime Kuma. (Note: this commenter also promotes their own Fortressa app-store service in the same post.)
A company that used PagerDuty eventually moved to a service providing physical, WiFi-connected pagers that looked like 1990s devices; the commenter found it "really cool."
"PagerDuty feels like abandonware. It hasn't changed in the last 4-5 years."

A developer integrating PagerDuty for their users complained about the integration keys. v1 and v2 Events API keys are random UUIDs that aren't interchangeable and can't be told apart, so users' v2 keys failed cryptically. They now try v1, then v2, which pollutes their error monitoring. Support's response was roughly "oh, uhhh... huh."
One user set their PagerDuty alert to the meow sound and jokingly calls their process "meow driven development": they don't like their phone meowing desperately.

PagerDuty is called "super expensive." The commenter says engineers rarely use the website, only the app or Slack to ack pages, and many bells and whistles aren't useful. They call $100/user/month on the enterprise plan "insane for what they offer" and say services like OpsGenie can undercut it.

Someone tasked with improving incident response compared PagerDuty with OpsGenie. They found OpsGenie at about 1/10 the cost with no significant feature gap, and PagerDuty's sales team couldn't articulate one. The sales rep said PagerDuty positions itself as the "luxury brand"; the commenter chose the generic option.
"Glad we got rid of pagerduty by hiring a couple folks outside of the US. Now everyone gets to sleep."

A long-time user says PagerDuty is "becoming worse and worse" over the years. They feel the company is adding features to keep developers busy instead of improving the core product, and wish it would "just deliver what it says on the tin."

A PagerDuty customer of 3 years at FarmLogs saw "literally zero innovation or development" and called it buggy and painful to use. Many times, acknowledging an issue mid-crisis failed and caused cascading pages to other engineers: "That's the one thing this product should do without fail."

A user of PagerDuty for years consolidated alerting from SolarWinds, Nagios and email into it, and got other admins off private emails to remove single points of failure. They say it was simple to configure. A text won't wake them, but PagerDuty's phone call does; they reject the call and open the app. "Love it."

A team was excited to replace their clunky phone, Slack and spreadsheet bot setup with PagerDuty. At $29/user/month, management won't approve it for a 50-person company where 30 people rotate on-call. They wished for more creative pricing.
